title: Comments on IBM’s Acquisition of the HRL Laboratories - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Doug Finke argues IBM's acquisition of HRL Laboratories is a rational 'insurance policy' against a quantum modality transition away from superconducting qubits, echoing Google/Quantum Circuits and IonQ/Oxford Ionics. The investable core is spin qubits' orders-of-magnitude smaller die area per qubit (potentially a million qubits on one chip) and their CMOS-process compatibility, which fits IBM's Anderon foundry and possibly SEEQC's SFQ control logic — with cost per qubit named as the eventual competitive battleground and Diraq already targeting $1/qubit.

insights.claim: New technologies commonly start with one implementation and later transition to a very different one offering better cost, performance, or quality — semiconductors moved germanium bipolar to silicon bipolar to bipolar ICs to NMOS to CMOS, displays moved CRT to plasma to LED to OLED, and locomotives moved steam to diesel electric.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for judging whether today's leading quantum modality is a durable moat or a transitional stage — the answer determines whether incumbency in superconducting qubits is worth paying for.
insights.locator: Technology Transitions

insights.claim: Superconducting qubits based on Josephson junctions remain the most mature quantum technology but are likely to be superseded in the long term by other modalities, even while enjoying a strong near- and medium-term run.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Frames superconducting-qubit pure plays as holding a time-limited lead — relevant to duration assumptions in any quantum hardware valuation.
insights.quote: This modality will still have a very good run in the near and medium term, much like CRTs and bipolar silicon transistors.
insights.locator: It is quite probably that we will see a similar phenomena occur

insights.claim: Even after a dominant technology emerges, niche applications persist for superseded approaches — CMOS dominates semiconductors while GaAs and SiC still hold specialized roles — implying quantum modalities will coexist rather than one fully eliminating the others.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Argues against a winner-take-all quantum modality outcome, which supports a basket rather than single-modality exposure.
insights.quote: There are still niche applications where other technologies, such as GaAs, SiC and others is still used.
insights.locator: And now CMOS is the dominant, but not exclusive technology

insights.claim: HRL's spin qubit technology has a die area per qubit orders of magnitude smaller than a superconducting qubit, which is the core physical argument for its long-term cost and form-factor advantage.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Die area per qubit is the metric that converts directly into cost per qubit at scale — the single most decision-relevant spec in the modality debate.
insights.quote: A significant advantage is that the die area per qubit is orders of magnitude smaller than a superconducting qubit.
insights.locator: The spin qubit technology being developed by HRL

insights.claim: Smaller die area could allow manufacturers to put as many as a million qubits or more on a single chip, avoiding the need to network many modules together.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Single-chip million-qubit integration would collapse the interconnect and networking cost stack that superconducting roadmaps must otherwise carry.
insights.quote: This can potentially allow manufacturers to put as many as a million qubits or more on a single chip, providing a significant cost and form factor advantage.
insights.locator: The spin qubit technology being developed by HRL

insights.claim: Spin qubits are the quantum modality most compatible with standard semiconductor processing, meaning progress can ride the existing chip manufacturing base rather than requiring bespoke process development.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Process compatibility is what lets a modality inherit decades of fab learning curve — a structural reason spin qubits could scale faster once funded.
insights.quote: In addition, the spin qubit technology is a modality that is the most compatible with standard semiconductor processing.
insights.locator: The spin qubit technology being developed by HRL

insights.claim: One of the biggest risks a large company faces is missing a technology transition — the pattern behind Kodak and digital photography, Blockbuster and streaming, and Blackberry and smartphones — so incumbents buy 'insurance policies' in adjacent modalities.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Explains why quantum M&A multiples can look irrational on near-term revenue — buyers are pricing transition insurance, not cash flows.
insights.quote: One of the biggest risks that any large company faces is to miss a technology transition.
insights.locator: Large Companies Like Insurance Policies

insights.claim: Google purchased Quantum Circuits Inc. last year, a deal that adds dual-rail cavity qubits to Google's traditional planar transmon approach even though both are superconducting.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Precedent transaction establishing that even within one modality, incumbents pay to own architectural variants.
insights.quote: last year Google purchased Quantum Circuits Inc.
insights.locator: We are starting to see this occur in quantum

insights.claim: Google is hedging across modalities beyond superconducting — it is an investor in neutral atom company QuEra and has set up its own neutral atom development program in Colorado.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Confirms multi-modality hedging is the standard playbook among the deepest-pocketed players, raising the strategic-buyer floor for neutral atom and spin qubit startups.
insights.quote: Google is also an investor in neutral atom company QuEra and has also set up its own neutral atom development program in Colorado.
insights.locator: Large Companies Like Insurance Policies

insights.claim: IonQ acquired Oxford Ionics to move from laser-based ion trap control to microwave-based control, another instance of an incumbent buying a different control approach within its own modality.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Third comparable in the same pattern — the M&A cluster suggests remaining independent modality specialists are acquisition candidates.
insights.quote: IonQ has acquired Oxford Ionics to take advantage of the latters ion trap technology controlled by microwaves energy from IonQ’s previous approach of implementing control using lasers.
insights.locator: Similarly, IonQ has acquired Oxford Ionics

themes.theme: IBM's ecosystem vs HRL's commercialization gap

insights.claim: IBM currently enjoys the highest customer revenue base of any quantum provider, built on the Qiskit SDK, education programs, university and software partnerships, web-accessible machines, and its existing classical enterprise relationships.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Establishes IBM as the revenue benchmark for the sector — a comparison point when quantum pure plays cite bookings or contract wins.
insights.quote: they currently enjoy the highest customer revenue base of any quantum provider
insights.locator: Taking Advantage of IBM’s Strong Quantum Ecosystem

insights.claim: HRL has strong spin qubit science — including impressive APS papers last March and its spinQICK control solution for electrostatically confined semiconductor spin qubits — but essentially no commercial go-to-market capability.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The tech-without-distribution profile is exactly what makes a lab cheap to buy and valuable inside a distribution-rich acquirer.
insights.quote: HRL has not traditionally developed the commercial go-to-market capabilities that IBM has been doing for a hundred years.
insights.locator: Conversely, HRL has not traditionally developed

insights.claim: Adoption of HRL's spinQICK control solution appears limited to a small number of universities, so IBM's distribution is the mechanism by which the technology could actually proliferate.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Quantifies the commercialization gap being closed — watch for spinQICK or spin-qubit access appearing in IBM's cloud fleet as the proof point.
insights.quote: But it is not clear that anyone besides a small number of universities are using this.
insights.locator: They have also developed a solution called spinQICK

insights.claim: IBM is partnering with the U.S. Department of Commerce to establish a quantum foundry called Anderon, which will heavily leverage the technology and facilities of the Albany NanoTech Complex.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Federally supported foundry capacity is a durable competitive asset — track Anderon tool-in and first wafers as a US quantum-manufacturing milestone.
insights.quote: IBM is partnering with the U.S. Department of Commerce to establish a quantum foundry called Anderon.
insights.locator: Leveraging Anderon

insights.claim: Anderon will have far more advanced wafer processing capability than HRL uses today, which is the specific mechanism by which the acquisition could accelerate spin qubit development.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The value creation here is process-node uplift, not IP alone — a testable claim if HRL device metrics jump after Anderon integration.
insights.quote: Anderon will certainly have much more advanced wafer processing capability than what HRL is using today and this will allow them to accelerate the development of their spin qubit technology.
insights.locator: Leveraging Anderon

insights.claim: One of the biggest challenges in scaling quantum processors to large qubit counts is routing all the control wires, which most superconducting systems still handle with coaxial or flex cables running down the dilution refrigerator.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Wiring, not qubit count, is a hard scaling ceiling — control-electronics suppliers are an under-appreciated bottleneck play in the quantum stack.
insights.quote: This eliminates routing a rat’s nest of wires from the room temperature control electronics down the dilution refrigerator.
insights.locator: Potential of Leveraging SFQ Logic from SEEQC

insights.claim: Single Flux Quantum logic is a more advanced alternative to cryoCMOS: because it is built on superconducting Josephson junctions it consumes orders of magnitude less heat and power, and it operates at speeds of tens of gigahertz.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Heat budget inside the fridge is the binding constraint on in-cryostat control — SFQ's power advantage is why it could displace cryoCMOS roadmaps.
insights.quote: In addition, SFQ logic is very fast and operates at speeds of 10’s of gigahertz.
insights.locator: An even more advanced version of logic than cryoCMOS

insights.claim: IBM is already partnering with SEEQC to use SFQ logic on DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative program, and may combine that SFQ logic with HRL's spin qubits in future processors.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A speculative but concrete combination to watch — SEEQC's relevance rises materially if IBM pairs SFQ control with spin qubits.
insights.quote: Although we don’t know for sure, IBM may decide to try to combine this SFQ logic with the HRL spin qubits for future processors.
insights.locator: Potential of Leveraging SFQ Logic from SEEQC

themes.theme: Cost per qubit as the coming battleground

insights.claim: Cost per qubit is not emphasized today because hardware teams are focused on just building something that works, but it will become decisive once users can choose between multiple providers.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Predicts the metric that will differentiate quantum vendors in the commercial phase — start tracking cost per qubit before the market does.
insights.quote: But, if we learn from the past, cost will ultimately play an important role when users have the ability to choose between multiple providers.
insights.locator: The Future Importance of Cost per Qubit

insights.claim: Australian spin qubit company Diraq is already promoting a goal of one dollar per qubit, setting an explicit cost benchmark for the industry.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A concrete $1/qubit target gives a yardstick to price any vendor's scaling claims against.
insights.quote: Australian spin qubit company Diraq is already promoting a goal of one dollar per qubit.
insights.locator: The Future Importance of Cost per Qubit

insights.claim: GQI projects that superconducting systems will not fit more than a few thousand qubits in a single module, forcing multi-system networking to go beyond that — a structural cost disadvantage versus single-chip spin qubit integration.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Quantifies the superconducting scaling ceiling; hitting $1/qubit while networking thousands of modules is the specific reason cost favors spin qubits long term.
insights.quote: GQI projects that superconducting systems won’t be able to fit more than a few thousand qubits in a single module before networking multiple systems will be required to go beyond that.
insights.locator: Due to die area per qubit and other considerations

insights.claim: Spin qubits will not quickly replace superconducting systems on IBM's roadmap — superconducting processors have a long and important role for the next several years as IBM brings Starling and Blue Jay to market.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Sets the horizon: the HRL deal is optionality for beyond Blue Jay, so near-term IBM quantum execution should still be judged on superconducting milestones.
insights.quote: The superconducting processors still have a long and important role ahead for the next several years as IBM brings their Starling and Blue Jay machines to market.
insights.locator: Conclusions

insights.claim: HRL also works in quantum sensors, advanced materials, MEMS, gallium nitride high-frequency electronics, vision systems, neuromorphic computing, and autonomous systems, and IBM's press release said very little about what happens to those assets.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A material unanswered question — these non-quantum assets could be divested, creating spin-out or carve-out opportunities in defense electronics.
insights.quote: Very little was mentioned in IBM’s press release about these other areas and it remains to be seen what IBM will do with these technologies from HRL.
insights.locator: But there is one other question about the acquisition

insights.claim: Integration risk is explicitly flagged: successfully absorbing a corporate acquisition always presents challenges, tempering the otherwise favorable strategic read on the IBM-HRL deal.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The bear case on the deal is execution, not strategy — watch HRL researcher retention and output cadence post-close.
insights.quote: Successfully integrating a new corporate acquisition can always present challenges and we wish IBM the best of luck in achieving their goals.
insights.locator: But there is one other question about the acquisition
